'''Bedford–Stuyvesant''' ({{IPAc-en|ˌ|b|ɛ|d|f|ər|d|_|ˈ|s|t|aɪ|v|ə|s|ə|n|t}} {{respell|BED|fərd|_|STY|və|sənt}}), colloquially known as '''Bed–Stuy''',<ref name="woodsworth">{{cite book |last=Woodsworth |first=Michael |title=Battle for Bed–Stuy: The Long War on Poverty in New York City |publisher=Harvard University Press |edition=illustrated |date=May 6, 2016 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rZK-CwAAQBAJ |isbn=9780674545069}}</ref> is a [[neighborhood]] in the northern section of the [[New York City borough]] of [[Brooklyn]]. It is bounded by [[Flushing Avenue]] to the north (bordering [[Williamsburg, Brooklyn|Williamsburg]]), Classon Avenue to the west (bordering [[Clinton Hill, Brooklyn|Clinton Hill]]), [[Broadway (Brooklyn)|Broadway]] to the east (bordering [[Bushwick, Brooklyn|Bushwick]] and [[East New York]]), and [[Atlantic Avenue (New York City)|Atlantic Avenue]] to the south (bordering [[Crown Heights]] and [[Brownsville, Brooklyn|Brownsville]]).<ref>[http://www.nyc.gov/html/dcp/pdf/lucds/bk3profile.pdf "Brooklyn Community District 3"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080514131351/http://www.nyc.gov/html/dcp/pdf/lucds/bk3profile.pdf |date=May 14, 2008}} (pdf). [[New York City Department of City Planning]]. December 2007. Accessed April 25, 2008.</ref> The main shopping street, Fulton Street, runs east–west the length of the neighborhood and intersects high-traffic north–south streets including [[Bedford Avenue]], [[Nostrand Avenue]], and Stuyvesant Avenue. Bedford–Stuyvesant contains four smaller neighborhoods: Bedford, Stuyvesant Heights, [[Ocean Hill, Brooklyn|Ocean Hill]], and [[Weeksville, Brooklyn|Weeksville]] (also part of Crown Heights). Part of [[Clinton Hill, Brooklyn|Clinton Hill]] was once considered part of Bedford–Stuyvesant.

Bedford–Stuyvesant has the largest collection of intact and largely untouched [[Victorian architecture]] in the United States, with roughly 8,800 buildings built before 1900.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/07/13/realestate/bedford-stuyvesant-diverse-and-changing.html|title=Bedford-Stuyvesant: Diverse and Changing|last=Gregor|first=Alison|date=July 9, 2014|work=The New York Times|access-date=July 16, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Its building stock includes many historic [[brownstone]]s, developed for the expanding upper-middle class from the 1890s to the late 1910s. They contain highly ornamental detailing throughout their interiors and have [[Classical architecture|classical architectural]] elements, such as brackets, [[Quoin (architecture)|quoins]], [[Fluting (architecture)|fluting]], [[finial]]s, and elaborate [[frieze]] and [[cornice]] banding.

Since the late 1930s, the neighborhood has been a major cultural center for Brooklyn's [[African Americans|African-American]] population. Following the construction of the [[IND Fulton Street Line|Fulton Street subway line]] ({{NYCS trains|Fulton}})<ref name="urbanology">Echanove, Matias. [http://urbanology.org/BedStuy/ "Bed-Stuy on the Move"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170916131340/http://urbanology.org/BedStuy/ |date=September 16, 2017 }}. Master thesis. Urban Planning Program. Columbia University. Urbanology.org. 2003.</ref> in 1936, African Americans left an overcrowded [[Harlem]] for greater housing availability in Bedford–Stuyvesant. From Bedford–Stuyvesant, African Americans have since moved into the surrounding areas of Brooklyn, such as [[East New York]], [[Crown Heights]], [[Brownsville, Brooklyn|Brownsville]], and [[Fort Greene, Brooklyn|Fort Greene]]. Since the early 2000s, Bedford–Stuyvesant has undergone significant gentrification, resulting in a dramatic demographic shift combined with increasing rent and real-estate prices.<ref>Gregor, Alison. [https://www.nytimes.com/2014/07/13/realestate/bedford-stuyvesant-diverse-and-changing.html "Living In: Bedford-Stuyvesant: Diverse and Changing"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', July 13, 2014. Accessed September 7, 2022. "To sum up Bedford-Stuyvesant as yet another stunning Brooklyn brownstone neighborhood falling victim to gentrification would be to deny the vitality and tenaciousness of a community with deep cultural and historic roots in the area.... From the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s, large numbers of African-American professionals moved into the neighborhood in what was perhaps the first wave of gentrification, said Tremaine Wright, a resident and the chairwoman of Brooklyn Community Board 3, who also owns the neighborhood coffee shop Common Grounds."</ref>

Bedford–Stuyvesant is mostly part of [[Brooklyn Community Board 3|Brooklyn Community District 3]]. Its primary [[ZIP Code]]s are 11205, 11206, 11216, 11221, 11233, and 11238.<ref name="NYCPlanning" /> Bedford–Stuyvesant is patrolled by the 79th and 81st Precincts of the [[New York City Police Department]].<ref name="NYPD 79th Precinct" /><ref name="NYPD 81st Precinct" /> Politically it is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s [[New York City's 36th City Council district|36th District]].
